INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE
Amicus curiae Federation for American Immigration
Reform (“FAIR”) is a nonprofit corporation and
membership organization that was founded in 1979 and
has its principal place of business in Washington, D.C.
FAIR’s mission is to advocate for immigration policy that
is in America’s best interests. FAIR has been involved in
hundreds of legal cases since 1980, either as a party or
amicus curiae , with the aim of advancing this mission. 1
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
Congress has authorized the Secretary of Homeland
Security or the Attorney General to “adjust to the status
of an alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence the
status of any alien granted asylum.” 8 U.S.C. § 1159(b).
Petitioners, whose grants of asylum were terminated
because they were convicted of serious crimes, seek
adjustment to permanent residence and urge this Court
to invoke the rule of lenity to resolve any ambiguity in
this statute in their favor. Brief for Petitioners (Pet. Br.)
at 40-44.
This Court should reject Petitioners’ invitation to
favor them at the expense of the American people. First of
all, immigration statutes are not punitive, so “lenity” has
no logical place in their interpretation. Second, in drafting
the asylum statute, Congress struck a balance between

offering protection to aliens from persecution abroad
and protecting the American people from potentially
dangerous aliens. The rule of lenity, however, is one-sided,
focusing here on only one of these purposes (extending
protection to aliens) at the expense of the other (protecting
the American people). It is thus inappropriate to apply it
in the asylum context.
The problem is especially acute in this case. Here,
applying the rule of lenity to decide this case in Petitioners’
favor would allow the termination of their grants of asylum
to be, in effect, reversed—and then some, as the status
of lawful permanent resident would give them many
additional benefits. At the same time, the adjustment
could only increase and extend the danger Petitioners have
been found to pose to public safety. The intensification of
potential public harm the application of the rule would
create makes that application doubly inappropriate here.
ARGUMENT
The rule of lenity should not apply in asylum cases
generally or to this case in particular.
There is no question that the United States has a right
inherent in its sovereignty to defend itself from foreign
dangers by controlling the admission of aliens. “It is an
accepted maxim of international law that every sovereign
nation has the power, as inherent in sovereignty, and
essential to self-preservation, to forbid the entrance of
foreigners within its dominions, or to admit them only in
such cases and upon such conditions as it may see fit to
prescribe.” Nishimura Ekiu v. United States , 142 U.S.
651, 659 (1892); see also Galvan v. Press , 347 U.S. 522,

3
531 (1954) (“Policies pertaining to the entry of aliens and
their right to remain here are . . . entrusted exclusively to
Congress . . . .”). Exercising this sovereign prerogative,
Congress has enacted a comprehensive and detailed
statutory scheme regulating immigration, the purpose
of which is to prevent and deter illegal immigration and
provide for the removal of certain undesirable aliens.
Congress has authorized the Secretary of Homeland
Security or the Attorney General to grant asylum to an
alien who is unable or unwilling to return to their country
of nationality “because of persecution or a well-founded
fear of persecution on account of race, religion, nationality,
membership in a particular social group, or political
opinion.” 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A) (defining refugee); see
also id. § 1158(b)(1)(A) (authorizing the grant of asylum to
an alien who is a refugee). Congress, however, established
limits on this authority to grant asylum. For example,
Congress precludes the government from granting
asylum to an alien who, “having been convicted by a final
judgment of a particularly serious crime, constitutes a
danger to the community of the United States.” 8 U.S.C.
§ 1158(b)(2)(A)(ii); see also id.  §  1158(b)(2)(A)(iii)-(v)
(barring asylum to aliens who commit serious nonpolitical
crimes outside the United States, who are a danger to the
security of the United States, or who are inadmissible
or deportable on certain terrorist grounds). To further
protect the American people, Congress authorized the
government to terminate a grant of asylum if an alien
meets any of the exceptions listed in § 1158(b)(2). 8 U.S.C.
§ 1158(c)(2). It is apparent from this scheme that Congress
sought to offer protection to aliens from persecution
abroad, but precluded this protection from being extended

4
to aliens who may be a danger to safety or welfare of the
American people.
The rule of lenity in the immigration context is often
traced to this Court’s decision in Fong Haw Tan v. Phelan,
in which the Court held that “because deportation is a
drastic measure and at times the equivalent of banishment
or exile,” and “since the stakes are considerable for the
individual,” “we will not assume that Congress meant to
trench on his freedom beyond that which is required by
the narrowest of several possible meanings of the words
used.” 333 U.S. 6, 9-10 (1948).
The rule marked a departure. Long before the rule
of lenity was announced in 1948, this Court had rejected
the premise upon which it is based. In 1893, this Court
recognized that:
The order of deportation is not a punishment
for crime. It is not a banishment, in the sense
in which that word is often applied to the
expulsion of a citizen from his country by way
of punishment. It is but a method of enforcing
the return to his own country of an alien who
has not complied with the conditions upon the
performance of which the government of the
nation, acting within its constitutional authority
and through the proper departments, has
determined that his continuing to reside here
shall depend.
Fong Yue Ting v. United States, 149 U.S. 698, 730 (1893).
Indeed, “[t]he right to expel aliens is a sovereign power
necessary to the safety of the country,” and an exercise

5
of this right seeks only “to rid the country of persons who
had shown by their career that their continued presence
here would not make for the safety or welfare of society.”
Mahler v. Eby , 264 U.S. 32, 39 (1924) (citing Fong Yue
Ting, 149 U.S. at 730).
Under the view of these cases, immigration restrictions
are enacted to protect the safety and welfare of the
American people, not to punish aliens for wrongdoing. If
there is no punishment, it is odd to speak of “lenity.”
Even if Fong Haw Tan  is regarded as amending
this view (or if the rule of “lenity” was misnamed in
the immigration context, and is really a rule of judicial
“compassion”), it is inappropriate to apply the rule in the
asylum context. Here, Petitioners had their grants of
asylum terminated because they had been convicted of
particularly serious crimes. Pet. App. at 3a, 6a. Congress
has made the judgment that those convicted of such
crimes are “a danger to the community of the United
States.” 8 U.S.C. § 1158(b)(2)(A)(ii). Because Congress
sought to protect the American people in authorizing
the government to terminate grants of asylum to such
individuals, and the rule of lenity counteracts this purpose,
the rule is out of place in the asylum context.
This is particularly so since Petitioners seek further
protection from removal through adjustment of status to
that of a lawful permanent resident. Lawful permanent
residents enjoy many of the same rights as American
citizens, such as the ability to work without restrictions,
own property, and receive certain public benefits. See,
e.g., 8 C.F .R. § 274a.12(a)(1) (establishing that lawful
permanent residents are authorized to work in the United

6
States due to their status). Lawful permanent residents
are also eligible to naturalize. 8 U.S.C. § 1427(a). By the
same token, Petitioner’s adjustment to that status would
only enhance and make more permanent the danger
they have been found to pose to public safety. It is thus
especially inappropriate to apply the rule of lenity in this
case.
CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, the judgment of the court
below should be affirmed.
